# Multer [![NPM Version][npm-version-image]][npm-url] [![NPM Downloads][npm-downloads-image]][npm-url] [![Build Status][ci-image]][ci-url] [![Test Coverage][test-image]][test-url] [![OpenSSF Scorecard Badge][ossf-scorecard-badge]][ossf-scorecard-visualizer] Multer is a node.js middleware for handling `multipart/form-data`, which is primarily used for uploading files. It is written on top of [busboy](https://github.com/mscdex/busboy) for maximum efficiency. **NOTE**: Multer will not process any form which is not multipart (`multipart/form-data`). ## Installation ```sh $ npm install multer ``` ## Usage Multer adds a `body` object and a `file` or `files` object to the `request` object. The `body` object contains the values of the text fields of the form, the `file` or `files` object contains the files uploaded via the form. Basic usage example: Don't forget the `enctype="multipart/form-data"` in your form. ```html
``` ```javascript const express = require('express') const multer = require('multer') const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' }) const app = express() app.post('/profile', upload.single('avatar'), function (req, res, next) { // req.file is the `avatar` file // req.body will hold the text fields, if there were any }) app.post('/photos/upload', upload.array('photos', 12), function (req, res, next) { // req.files is array of `photos` files // req.body will contain the text fields, if there were any }) const uploadMiddleware = upload.fields([{ name: 'avatar', maxCount: 1 }, { name: 'gallery', maxCount: 8 }]) app.post('/cool-profile', uploadMiddleware, function (req, res, next) { // req.files is an object (String -> Array) where fieldname is the key, and the value is array of files // // e.g. // req.files['avatar'][0] -> File // req.files['gallery'] -> Array // // req.body will contain the text fields, if there were any }) ``` In case you need to handle a text-only multipart form, you should use the `.none()` method: ```javascript const express = require('express') const app = express() const multer = require('multer') const upload = multer() app.post('/profile', upload.none(), function (req, res, next) { // req.body contains the text fields }) ``` Here's an example on how multer is used in a HTML form. Take special note of the `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and `name="uploaded_file"` fields: ```html
``` Then in your javascript file you would add these lines to access both the file and the body. It is important that you use the `name` field value from the form in your upload function. This tells multer which field on the request it should look for the files in. If these fields aren't the same in the HTML form and on your server, your upload will fail: ```javascript const multer = require('multer') const upload = multer({ dest: './public/data/uploads/' }) app.post('/stats', upload.single('uploaded_file'), function (req, res) { // req.file is the name of your file in the form above, here 'uploaded_file' // req.body will hold the text fields, if there were any console.log(req.file, req.body) }); ``` Complete client-side and server-side examples (browser `FormData` uploads of a blob and of an image) are in the [`examples/`](examples/) folder. ## API ### File information Each file contains the following information: Key | Description | Note --- | --- | --- `fieldname` | Field name specified in the form | `originalname` | Name of the file on the user's computer, or the full path when `preservePath: true` | `encoding` | Encoding type of the file | `mimetype` | Mime type of the file | `size` | Size of the file in bytes | `destination` | The folder to which the file has been saved | `DiskStorage` `filename` | The name of the file within the `destination` | `DiskStorage` `path` | The full path to the uploaded file | `DiskStorage` `buffer` | A `Buffer` of the entire file | `MemoryStorage` ### `multer(opts)` Multer accepts an options object, the most basic of which is the `dest` property, which tells Multer where to upload the files. In case you omit the options object, the files will be kept in memory and never written to disk. By default, Multer will rename the files so as to avoid naming conflicts. The renaming function can be customized according to your needs. The following are the options that can be passed to Multer. Key | Description --- | --- `defCharset` | Default character set to use for text field values that do not declare one. Default: `'utf8'` `defParamCharset` | Default character set to use for values of part header parameters (e.g. filename) that are not extended parameters (that contain an explicit charset). Default: `'latin1'` `dest` or `storage` | Where to store the files `fileFilter` | Function to control which files are accepted `fileHwm` | `highWaterMark` of each file stream (`file.stream`). Default: busboy's default `highWaterMark` | `highWaterMark` of the multipart parser stream. Default: busboy's default `limits` | Limits of the uploaded data `preservePath` | Keep the full client-supplied path in `file.originalname` instead of just the base name `streamHandler` | Function that feeds the request body to busboy; defaults to `req.pipe(busboy)` In an average web app, only `dest` might be required, and configured as shown in the following example. ```javascript const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' }) ``` When `preservePath` is enabled, Multer passes the incoming filename through with any path segments provided by the client. This is exposed as `file.originalname`; it does not change the destination folder, create directories, or sanitize the path for you. `file.originalname` is always client-supplied and should be treated as untrusted; with `preservePath` it additionally contains the path segments the client sent. Normalize or validate it before using it in a custom `filename` or storage engine. If you want more control over your uploads, you'll want to use the `storage` option instead of `dest`. Multer ships with storage engines `DiskStorage` and `MemoryStorage`; More engines are available from third parties. #### `.single(fieldname)` Accept a single file with the name `fieldname`. The single file will be stored in `req.file`. #### `.array(fieldname[, maxCount])` Accept an array of files, all with the name `fieldname`. Optionally error out if more than `maxCount` files are uploaded. The array of files will be stored in `req.files`. Files skipped by `fileFilter` do not count towards `maxCount`. Use `limits.files` to bound how many files are read from a request. #### `.fields(fields)` Accept a mix of files, specified by `fields`. An object with arrays of files will be stored in `req.files`. `fields` should be an array of objects with `name` and optionally a `maxCount`. Example: ```javascript [ { name: 'avatar', maxCount: 1 }, { name: 'gallery', maxCount: 8 } ] ``` #### `.none()` Accept only text fields. If any file upload is made, error with code `LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE` will be issued. #### `.any()` Accepts all files that come over the wire. An array of files will be stored in `req.files`. **WARNING:** Make sure that you always handle the files that a user uploads. Never add multer as a global middleware since a malicious user could upload files to a route that you didn't anticipate. Only use this function on routes where you are handling the uploaded files. ### `storage` #### `DiskStorage` The disk storage engine gives you full control on storing files to disk. ```javascript const crypto = require('crypto') const storage = multer.diskStorage({ destination: function (req, file, cb) { cb(null, '/tmp/my-uploads') }, filename: function (req, file, cb) { crypto.randomBytes(16, function (err, raw) { if (err) return cb(err) cb(null, file.fieldname + '-' + raw.toString('hex')) }) } }) const upload = multer({ storage: storage }) ``` There are three options available: `destination`, `filename` and `flush`. All of them except `flush` are functions that determine where the file should be stored. `destination` is used to determine within which folder the uploaded files should be stored. This can also be given as a `string` (e.g. `'/tmp/uploads'`). If no `destination` is given, the operating system's default directory for temporary files is used. **Note:** You are responsible for creating the directory when providing `destination` as a function. When passing a string, multer will make sure that the directory is created for you. `filename` is used to determine what the file should be named inside the folder. If no `filename` is given, each file will be given a random name that doesn't include any file extension. **Note:** Multer will not append any file extension for you, your function should return a filename complete with a file extension. Each function gets passed both the request (`req`) and some information about the file (`file`) to aid with the decision. Note that `req.body` might not have been fully populated yet. It depends on the order that the client transmits fields and files to the server. For understanding the calling convention used in the callback (needing to pass null as the first param), refer to [Node.js error handling](https://web.archive.org/web/20220417042018/https://www.joyent.com/node-js/production/design/errors) `flush` is an optional boolean. When set to `true`, the file data is flushed to disk with an `fsync` call before the upload handler runs, which prevents data loss if the process or the system crashes while the data is still sitting in the operating system's page cache. It is disabled by default because forcing a disk flush on every upload has a performance cost. Note that this syncs the file contents only; if the new directory entry must survive a crash as well, fsync the destination directory yourself. #### `MemoryStorage` The memory storage engine stores the files in memory as `Buffer` objects. It doesn't have any options. ```javascript const storage = multer.memoryStorage() const upload = multer({ storage: storage }) ``` When using memory storage, the file info will contain a field called `buffer` that contains the entire file. **WARNING**: Uploading very large files, or relatively small files in large numbers very quickly, can cause your application to run out of memory when memory storage is used. ### `limits` An object specifying the size limits of the following optional properties. Multer passes this object into busboy directly, and the details of the properties can be found on [busboy's page](https://github.com/mscdex/busboy#exports). `limits` can also be a function that receives the request and returns such an object. It is called once per request, before parsing starts, so limits can depend on e.g. the authenticated user: ```javascript const upload = multer({ limits: function (req) { return { fileSize: req.user.maxUploadSize } } }) ``` Limits apply to the whole request; there is no per-file limit. To restrict individual files by type or name, use `fileFilter` or a custom storage engine. The following integer values are available: Key | Description | Default --- | --- | --- `fieldNameSize` | Max field name size | Infinity `fieldSize` | Max field value size (in bytes) | 1MB `fields` | Max number of non-file fields | Infinity `fileSize` | For multipart forms, the max file size (in bytes) | Infinity `files` | For multipart forms, the max number of file fields | Infinity `parts` | For multipart forms, the max number

commits.author: UlisesGascon
commits.message:
fix: don't add a failed upload to the abort cleanup list (#1489)

When a file hits the fileSize limit (aborting the upload) and its storage
engine then reports an error, nothing was stored and the file has no path.
Such a file must not be added to the abort cleanup list, otherwise the
storage _removeFile runs on a path-less file (DiskStorage unlinks an
undefined path). Only record a successfully stored file, and add a
regression test.

commits.author: kilisamemarisaaa
commits.message:
test: cover storage engine _removeFile invocation semantics (#1460)

Adds regression tests for the storage engine _removeFile contract raised in
#1293: _handleFile's cb(null, info) is merged onto the same file object that
_removeFile receives (fileInfo = { ...file, ...info } in make-middleware.js),
_removeFile is only invoked when the request aborts after a file was stored,
and a successful request never calls it.

Covers:
- no _removeFile call on a successful request
- _removeFile receives the merged file object (path from _handleFile info)
  when a later file exceeds the file size limit
- stored files are cleaned up when fileFilter errors on a later file
- memory storage engine calls _removeFile on the error cleanup path

Co-authored-by: EvoX <[REDACTED:email]>
Co-authored-by: Ulises Gascon <[REDACTED:email]>

fix: do not consume maxCount for files skipped by fileFilter (#1426)

wrappedFileFilter decremented the field's remaining-count before the user
fileFilter ran, so a file skipped via cb(null, false) still consumed a
slot. With e.g. .array('docs', 1), a skipped file made the next accepted
file on the same field fail with LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE, even though zero
files had been stored. Decrement only after the filter accepts the file.

pulls.title: fix: don't call next() again when the request closes after busboy fails to start
pulls.body:
When the Busboy constructor throws, for example on `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` with no boundary or on `multipart/mixed`, the middleware calls `next(err)` but leaves `isDone` false. The `error`/`aborted`/`close` listeners on `req` are already attached at that point. If the client then disconnects, or the app destroys the request to stop reading it, `handleRequestFailure` runs and `next` is called a second time:

```
before: ['Multipart: Boundary not found', 'Request aborted']
after:  ['Multipart: Boundary not found']
```

The fix sets `isDone` in the catch block. `done()` and `handleRequestFailure` already check that flag, so the listeners stay in place but no longer call `next` again. The PR adds a regression test next to the existing busboy constructor test and an Unreleased changelog line.

- Ran: `npm test`, 172 passing, 2 pending. On main the new test fails with an extra `'Request closed'`.
- Ran: `npm run lint`, clean.
- Checked: a plain http server receiving a boundary-less upload followed by a client disconnect now gets one callback. An aborted upload with a valid boundary still reports `Request aborted` once.

Fixes #1492

pulls.title: fix: only act on the first accept or reject from fileFilter
pulls.body:
If a `fileFilter` calls its callback more than once, the middleware acts on every call (`lib/make-middleware.js:358`). The usual way this happens is a missing `return`:

```js
function fileFilter (req, file, cb) {
  if (!file.mimetype.startsWith('image/')) {
    cb(null, false)
  }
  cb(null, true)
}
```

The reject removes the placeholder and resumes the stream (line 369). Then the accept goes down the accept path (line 380) and hands the same stream to `storage._handleFile` (line 392). So the file the filter rejected gets stored anyway. With `.single()` it shows up as `req.file`. With `.array()` or `.fields()` it is stored but missing from `req.files`, so `DiskStorage` leaves it on disk with nothing pointing at it. The reject has already handed back the `maxCount` slot (`index.js:137`), so these files are not counted against `maxCount` either. The other orders break too:

- A reject after an accept removes the placeholder of a file that is still being stored, so the file drops out of `req.files`. With `DiskStorage` it also stays on disk.
- Two accepts call `_handleFile` twice and increment `pendingWrites` twice. `decrementPendingWrites` (line 313) only decrements once per file, so `next()` is never called.

`index.js` already treats the first call as the decision for the `maxCount` slot (`settled`, lines 133 to 141). This change makes the middleware do the same: it ignores any accept or reject after the first. Errors are still handled whenever they arrive. That keeps the existing "should not crash when fileFilter invokes the callback more than once" test (reject, then error) reporting its error, and an accept followed by an error still aborts the request and removes the stored file.

Three new tests in `test/file-filter.js` cover each order:

- reject then accept with `.single()`: `req.file` stays undefined
- accept then reject with `.array()`: the file stays in `req.files`
- two accepts: `_handleFile` runs once and the request finishes

I could not run mocha or `npm run lint`, because the npm registry is unreachable from my environment and I could not install the dependencies. Instead, I ran the test files on Node 22.23.3 with small stand-ins I wrote for busboy, append-field, type-is, form-data, express, fs-temp and rimraf, driven by a minimal describe/it runner. On `main`, all three new tests fail: the first gets the rejected 122-byte file in `req.file`, the second gets `0 !== 1` for `req.files.length`, and the third times out. With the change, all three pass. I could run every test file except `express-integration.js` and `fields.js`, and none of the existing tests change result: 153 passing and 3 failing before, 156 passing after, plus 2 pending (the Linux-only `/proc/self/fd` tests). I also ran a separate script with `DiskStorage` and `.array('docs', 1)`. On `main`, an upload with two rejected files and one accepted file left all three files on disk, with only the accepted one in `req.files`. With the change, only the accepted file was written. CI is the real check for the mocha run and lint.

pulls.title: feat!: enforce default fieldNestingDepth of 32
pulls.body:
The v3 constructor already enforces default values for `fieldNameSize`, `fieldSize`, `fields`, `fileSize`, `files`, and `headerPairs`. `fieldNestingDepth` was the last documented limit without an enforced default (gated by `?? Infinity` in the constructor), leaving deeply-nested field names as the one unbounded per-field allocation path.

This adds a default of `32`, matching the shape of the other limits:

- Well above legitimate form usage (typically 3-5 levels of nesting).
- Small enough to bound the per-bracket `append-field` allocation cost.
- Applications that need more can opt in with `limits.fieldNestingDepth`.

The existing "should allow unlimited nesting by default" test is replaced with two tests: one asserting the default is enforced (33 brackets rejects), and one asserting explicit opt-in to a higher limit still works.

**Breaking change** for next major. Consumers relying on unbounded nesting must set `limits.fieldNestingDepth` explicitly.

pulls.title: fix: clean up uploaded files after flush failure
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes #1504.

When DiskStorage is configured with `flush: true`, failures during `fs.open()`, `fs.fsync()`, or `fs.close()` can leave uploaded files on disk.

This PR uses the existing `_removeFile()` method to clean up the stored file before propagating the original flush error.

It also avoids duplicate cleanup when a request abort has already initiated file removal.

## Changes

- Clean up stored files after flush failures.
- Preserve the original flush error.
- Avoid duplicate file removal during request aborts.
- Add four regression tests covering `fs.open()`, `fs.fsync()`, `fs.close()`, and abort-related cleanup.

## Testing

- `npm test` — 175 passing, 2 pending
- `npm run lint` — passed
- `git diff --check` — passed

Tested locally on macOS with Node.js v24.22.1.

## Known limitation

If file removal itself fails, the original flush error is preserved, but the cleanup error is not included in `storageErrors`. This change attempts file removal but cannot guarantee cleanup when the underlying filesystem rejects the operation.

pulls.title: fix: a fileFilter or filename function that throws crashes the server
pulls.body:
Closes #904

`fileFilter` and `storage._handleFile` are called from busboy's `'file'` event, which fires while busboy is processing a chunk piped from `req`. On Node 22 and earlier nothing on that stack catches exceptions, so if the filter, or a `DiskStorage` `destination` / `filename` function, throws instead of calling back with an error, the exception is uncaught and the process exits. Express can't help, because by then the middleware call has already returned.

Node 24 changed `Readable.prototype.pipe()` to catch a throw from `dest.write()` and destroy the destination with it (nodejs/node#55270), so there the error already reaches `next(err)` through busboy's `'error'` event. multer supports Node >= 10.16 and Node 22 is still an LTS line, so this fixes the crash there and gives every supported version the same behavior instead of depending on the Node version.

The usual way to hit it is code that trusts the client-supplied name:

```js
const storage = multer.diskStorage({
  destination: 'uploads/',
  filename (req, file, cb) {
    // TypeError for a file named "README" with no extension
    cb(null, file.originalname.match(/\.(\w+)$/)[1] + '-' + Date.now())
  }
})
```

On Node 22, one upload of a file without an extension brings the server down. In #904 @jonchurch suggested catching it in the `'file'` handler and aborting with the error, and that is what this does. A throwing `limits` function already goes to `next(err)` the same way (`test/limits-function.js`).

The change:

- The `fileFilter` call and the `storage._handleFile` call are each wrapped in `try`/`catch`. A synchronous throw is handled as if the error had been passed to the callback, so it goes through the existing paths: the placeholder is removed, pending writes settle, files already stored for the request are removed, and `next(err)` is called once.
- If the middleware has already called `next()` when the exception arrives, it is rethrown unchanged. At that point it can come from the application's own handler (a storage engine that calls back synchronously), and multer should not swallow it or clean up files the route is using.
- The two callbacks became named functions (`onFileFiltered`, `onFileStored`) so they could be called from the `catch`. Their bodies are unchanged, which keeps the diff to the call sites.

A `destination` function that calls back asynchronously and then has `filename` throw is still outside multer's stack, so it is not covered; that has to be caught in the application.

Tests, all failing on `main` under Node 22 with an uncaught exception and passing with the change (on Node 24 and later they already pass on `main`, because of the `pipe()` change):

- `test/file-filter.js`: a filter that throws reaches the callback with its error and `req.file` stays undefined
- `test/disk-storage.js`: a throwing `destination` function, and a `filename` function that throws a `TypeError` on a name with no extension (the upload dir stays empty)
- `test/disk-storage.js`: with `.any()`, a filter that throws on the second file still removes the first file, which was already written to disk

`npm test` passes on Node 22.23.4 and 26.7.0, and `npm run lint` passes.

This touches the same `fileFilter` callback as #1491, but not the same lines; whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase.

pulls.title: fix: remove aborted uploads through the objects in req.files
pulls.body:
When an upload fails after some files were already stored (a later file hits `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`, `LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE`, a `fileFilter` error and so on), multer removes the stored files before calling `next(err)`. With `single()` the error handler then sees `req.file` without its `path` (disk) or `buffer` (memory), because `req.file` is the same object multer passes to `_removeFile`.

With `array()`, `fields()` and `any()` that is not the case. `replacePlaceholder` copies the file's properties onto the placeholder in `req.files`, but `uploadedFiles` keeps the original object. So on error:

- disk storage: `req.files[i].path` still points at a file that has just been unlinked
- memory storage: `req.files[i].buffer` still holds the whole file, although `_removeFile` already "freed" it
- `err.storageErrors[i].file` is a different object from the entry in `req.files` (the existing test for `single()` asserts `err.storageErrors[0].file === req.file`)

Repro (disk storage):

```js
const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' }).fields([{ name: 'a', maxCount: 1 }])
// send a file in `a`, then a file in `b`
// err.code === 'LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE', uploads/ is empty,
// but req.files.a[0].path is still 'uploads/<name>'
```

The fix has `replacePlaceholder` return the object it stored in `req.file` / `req.files`, and the middleware tracks that object in `uploadedFiles`. Removal then goes through the same object the error handler sees, so all strategies behave like `single()` already does. The object passed to `_removeFile` still carries the info returned by `_handleFile`, so the existing `_removeFile` tests are unaffected.

Tests:

- disk storage: `fields()` + `LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE` leaves `req.files.tiny0[0]` without `path`/`filename`/`destination`, and the upload dir empty
- memory storage: `array(name, 1)` + a second file leaves `req.files[0].buffer` undefined
- error handling: `err.storageErrors[0].file === req.files.tiny0[0]` for `fields()`

All three fail on `main` and pass with the change; the full suite and `standard` pass.

pulls.title: docs: fix limit examples and defaults that disagree with the code
pulls.body:
I checked the limits docs against the code on `main` (2c380d0) and found four places where they disagree. I ran a small script against a local checkout for each one.

**1. `fieldNestingDepth` example in the Security section**

The Security list says to use `3` for `a[b][c]`. The limits table and the JSDoc both say `a[b][c]` has 2 levels, and the check counts `[` characters. With `fieldNestingDepth: 2`, `a[b][c]` is accepted. With `1`, it fails with `LIMIT_FIELD_NESTING`. So the minimum for `a[b][c]` is 2.

**2. `fieldArrayIndexLimit` example in the Security section**

The Security list says to use `100` for `a[99]`. The limit is the largest index accepted (`Number(index) > limit` is rejected, and the existing test "should allow an index at exactly the limit" covers this). With `fieldArrayIndexLimit: 99`, `a[99]` is accepted. With `98`, it fails with `LIMIT_FIELD_ARRAY_INDEX`. So the value for `a[99]` is 99.

**3. `fieldNameSize` default in the JSDoc**

The `Limits` typedef in `index.js` says `[fieldNameSize=100]`. busboy only reads `fieldNameSize` in its urlencoded parser, and multer only checks it when the caller sets it. With no limits, a 5000-byte field name is accepted. The README table already says the default is `Infinity`, so I changed the JSDoc to match.

**4. `headerPairs` is not read by busboy 1.x**

The README and JSDoc list `headerPairs` as a limit. busboy 1.x hardcodes `MAX_HEADER_PAIRS = 2000` in `lib/types/multipart.js` and never reads `limits.headerPairs`. I sent a file part with four headers (`Content-Disposition`, `Content-Type`, `Content-Transfer-Encoding`, `X-Extra`) with `headerPairs` set to 0, 1 and 2. All three requests succeeded with `mimetype: 'image/png'` and `encoding: 'binary'`, so every header was parsed. I kept the 2000 default in the table and added a short note that the option is currently ignored, since someone setting it for DoS protection would otherwise assume it works.

**Testing**

- `npm run lint` passes.
- `npm test` passes (173 passing).
- The verification script output:

```
fieldNestingDepth=2, a[b][c] -> OK
fieldNestingDepth=1, a[b][c] -> ERROR LIMIT_FIELD_NESTING
fieldArrayIndexLimit=99, a[99] -> OK
fieldArrayIndexLimit=98, a[99] -> ERROR LIMIT_FIELD_ARRAY_INDEX
no limits, 5000-byte field name -> OK
fieldNameSize=100, 101-byte name -> ERROR LIMIT_FIELD_KEY
headerPairs=1 -> OK { mimetype: 'image/png', encoding: 'binary', originalname: 'a.png' }
headerPairs=2 -> OK { mimetype: 'image/png', encoding: 'binary', originalname: 'a.png' }
headerPairs=0 -> OK { mimetype: 'image/png', encoding: 'binary', originalname: 'a.png' }
```

I'm happy to drop the `headerPairs` note if you would rather handle that a different way, for example by removing the option from the docs.

pulls.title: fix(docs): handle string destination in storage engine template
pulls.body:
Closes #1278

<!-- Drafted by an agent run; please review carefully before merging. -->

## Repo
expressjs/multer

## Issue
https://github.com/expressjs/multer/issues/1278

## Root cause
The `StorageEngine.md` custom storage template assigned `opts.destination`
directly to `this.getDestination` and then invoked it as a function in
`_handleFile`. If a user follows the convention used by `DiskStorage` and
passes `destination` as a string path, the template throws a TypeError
because a string is not callable.

## Fix
Updated the `MyCustomStorage` constructor in `StorageEngine.md` to mirror
the behavior of `storage/disk.js`: when `opts.destination` is a string,
wrap it in a `function ($0, $1, cb) { cb(null, opts.destination) }`
adapter; otherwise fall back to the function-or-default assignment.

## Regression test
None. The change is documentation-only (`StorageEngine.md`); the existing
`storage/disk.js` already correctly handles string destinations and is
covered by `test/disk-storage.js`.

## Risk
trivial

## Verification
skipped: documentation-only change with no executable code path; existing
disk-storage tests cover the equivalent runtime behavior the docs now
reflect.

pulls.title: fix: allow a field value exactly at the fieldSize limit
pulls.body:
A text field whose value is exactly `limits.fieldSize` bytes is rejected with `LIMIT_FIELD_VALUE`. Every other limit in multer is inclusive: `fileSize`, `parts`, `files`, `fields` and `fieldNameSize` all accept a request sitting exactly on the limit. Set `limits: { fieldSize: 5 }`, send the 5 byte value `hello`, and you get `err.code === 'LIMIT_FIELD_VALUE'` with `err.field === 'field0'`, while `hell` goes through. Busboy also defaults `fieldSize` to a finite 1MB, so `multer().none()` with no limits rejects exactly 1048576 bytes, against `README.md:307`, "Max field value size (in bytes) | 1MB".

Busboy marks a field part truncated as soon as the value reaches the limit, at `node_modules/busboy/lib/types/multipart.js:502`, where `fieldSize === fieldSizeLimit` sets `partTruncated = true`. Multer turns the resulting `valueTruncated` straight into an error at `lib/make-middleware.js:262`. It already compensates for this busboy convention in the block at `lib/make-middleware.js:92` to `113`, but only for two of the three limits: line 107 passes `limits.fileSize + 1`, line 111 passes `limits.parts + 1`, and `fieldSize` is never adjusted. Those two came in with `fix: allow files at exact fileSize limit` and `fix: allow exactly limits.parts parts`. Busboy's finite default sits at `multipart.js:251`.

The change gives `fieldSize` the same treatment. `busboyLimits` is now built unconditionally from the caller's limits, and `fieldSize` goes to busboy one higher, so truncation is reported only once the limit is genuinely exceeded. That adjustment runs even with no caller limits, so a new `DEFAULT_FIELD_SIZE` constant pins busboy's 1MB in multer rather than inheriting it; if busboy changes its default, multer's effective limit no longer tracks it. I checked the edge cases by running them: `Infinity` passes through untouched and a 3MB value is accepted, `0` accepts an empty value and rejects one byte, and `null` falls back to the same 1MB busboy uses.

Verification on Node 22.23.2, macOS 26.2. With only the four new tests applied to unmodified `main`, `npx mocha --reporter spec --exit --check-leaks test/error-handling.js --grep "fieldSize"` gives 2 passing and 2 failing, both `AssertionError: ifError got unwanted exception: Field value too long`; with the `lib` change all four pass. The full suite goes from 165 passing to 169 passing, 2 pending and 0 failing either way, and `npm run lint` is clean. The third and fourth tests post 1048576 and 1048577 bytes through `multer().none()`, the true zero-options default, which the explicit `fieldSize: 5` tests cannot reach. The fourth also passes on `main`, so it pins the default rather than regressing.

pulls.body: Busboy emits its `limit` event once a file reaches exactly `fileSize` bytes, so multer rejects uploads that are exactly at the limit with `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`. This passes `fileSize + 1` down to Busboy so the limit only triggers when the size is genuinely exceeded. Closes #1348.

pulls.title: fix: decode escaped field names, not just filenames
pulls.body:
`decodeFormDataName` reverses the WHATWG escaping of `%0A`, `%0D` and `%22`, and its own comment says the rule covers "field names and filenames". It was only applied to `filename`. Busboy leaves both escaped, so `req.body` keys, `file.fieldname` and `err.field` all carried the raw escapes.

Measured against the unpatched tree:

```
body keys                        -> ["a%22b"]        expected a"b
upload.single('a"b') + that file -> LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE
originalname                     -> q".txt           already correct
```

So an `<input name='a"b' type=file>` upload is rejected outright, and the only way to accept it was to register the escaped spelling.

`fieldNameSize` now measures the name as it arrived, since decoding shortens it and measuring the decoded form would quietly weaken that limit. `decodeFormDataName` itself is untouched, so the deliberate "never `decodeURIComponent`" property still holds and `50%.pdf` stays intact.

Six new tests, two of which pass before the change as controls (a name with no escapes, and a literal percent sign). The other four fail on the unpatched tree. Each of the two call sites was neutered independently to confirm both are load-bearing.

Suite: 132 passing before, 138 after, 2 pending, no failures either side; `standard` exits 0.

This is the field-name half of #1421, which fixed the filename half.

pulls.title: fix(tests): keep Git from rewriting fixture line endings on Windows
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/expressjs/multer/issues/181

> Replaces #1449, reopened only to correct the source branch name. Same commit (`fcff40e`), same diff, body unchanged.

## Symptom

On a clean clone on Windows, `npm test` gives **12 failing / 71 passing** before any code is touched:

```
AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly equal:
1803 !== 1778
```

## Cause

`test/files/` holds opaque upload payloads whose exact byte size the suite hardcodes, and nothing marked them as binary. With `core.autocrlf=true` — Git's default on Windows — checkout rewrites LF to CRLF in the text-like fixtures:

| fixture | committed blob | on disk after checkout |
|---|---|---|
| `medium.dat` | 13196 | 13386 |
| `small0.dat` | 1778 | 1803 |
| `small1.dat` | 315 | 329 |
| `tiny0.dat` | 122 | 128 |
| `empty.dat`, `tiny1.dat` | 0, 7 | unchanged (no line terminators) |
| `large.jpg` | 2413677 | unchanged (Git detects it as binary) |

The committed blobs already hold exactly the LF bytes the tests expect — `1778` for `small0.dat`, matching every `assert.strictEqual(..., 1778)`. Only the checkout conversion is wrong.

## Fix

One `.gitattributes` marking `test/files/**` as binary. Because the blobs are already correct, suppressing the end-of-line conversion is sufficient on its own — the fixtures are not modified, so the hardcoded sizes stay valid and there is no fixture churn to review.

This follows the second option @jonchurch [laid out on the issue](https://github.com/expressjs/multer/issues/181#issuecomment-577471155) — "changing the behavior of git with a `.gitattributes` file" — rather than @LinusU's original suggestion of regenerating the fixtures as random binary data. Both stop the conversion; this one leaves the recorded sizes and the fixtures themselves untouched. `binary` also implies `-diff`, which is what you want for opaque payloads.

I kept this to a single file on purpose: the previous attempt, #832, was closed after the feedback that it "changes too many things to be easily evaluated".

## Deliberately unchanged

**The 12th failure is a different bug and is not touched here.** `Functionality > should rename the destination directory to a different directory` asserts `req.files[0].path.indexOf('/testforme-') >= 0`, hardcoding a forward slash as the path separator, so it can never match a Windows path regardless of line endings. It fails before and after this change. It deserves its own issue and PR.

## Testing

Windows 11, Node v24.18.0, `core.autocrlf=true`.

| | passing | failing |
|---|---|---|
| clean clone, before | 71 | 12 |
| with this change | 79 | 1 |

The 11 fixed failures span `disk-storage`, `functionality`, `memory-storage`, `reuse-middleware` and `select-field`; the 1 remaining is the path-separator assertion above.

Verified end to end rather than only in place: after pushing this branch I made a **fresh `git clone` of it** on Windows and confirmed every fixture arrives at its committed size with no CR bytes, then ran `npm install && npm test` in that new clone — 79 passing, 1 failing. `npm run lint` (`standard`) is clean.

I have no way to run the macOS or Linux jobs locally; those platforms do not convert line endings on checkout, so their behaviour is unchanged by this, and CI is the authority.

pulls.title: feat(disk-storage): support opt-in flush for durable uploads (#1381)
pulls.body:
Closes #1381.

## Why

As reported in #1381, the disk storage pipes the uploaded file into a vanilla \`fs.createWriteStream\` and reports the upload as successful the moment the stream finishes. On Linux (and any OS with a write-back page cache) the bytes can still be sitting in kernel buffers when the request handler returns, a power loss or crash at the wrong moment leaves the file truncated or zero-length, but the HTTP response already claimed success.

Node.js 20.10 / 21.0 added a \`flush\` option to \`fs.createWriteStream\` that calls \`fdatasync()\` on the file descriptor before the stream closes, which is exactly what this workflow needs.

## Change

Expose \`flush\` as an opt-in \`DiskStorage\` option:

\`\`\`js
multer.diskStorage({
  destination: './uploads',
  flush: true
})
\`\`\`

- Default stays \`false\`, so existing users get the exact same buffered-write behavior and the same throughput, no perf regression.
- When \`flush\` is \`true\`, the option is forwarded as \`fs.createWriteStream(path, { flush: true })\`. On runtimes older than Node 20.10, \`createWriteStream\` silently ignores the option, which matches the documented upstream behavior.
- No change to \`_removeFile\` or error handling.

## Tests

Added two regression tests in \`test/disk-storage.js\`:

1. With \`flush: true\`, the test wraps \`fs.createWriteStream\` and asserts it was called with \`{ flush: true }\` while the upload still round-trips at the expected size.
2. Without \`flush\`, \`createWriteStream\` is still called with no options, verifies the default behavior is unchanged.

Full \`npm test\` suite: **74/74 passing**.

issues.body:
## Environment information

**Version**: Multer version (^2.2.0)

**Platform**: macOS

**Node.js version**: To be confirmed

**Any other relevant information**:
- Configured Multer file size limit: `10 * 1024 * 1024` (10 MiB / 10,485,760 bytes).
- Actual uploaded file size: `10,485,760` bytes.
- Multer error code: `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`.

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

1. Create a DOCX file with an exact size of `10,485,760` bytes.
2. Configure Multer with the following limits:

   ```javascript
   limits: {
     fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
     files: 1,
   }
   ```

3. Upload the file using the configured Multer middleware.
4. Observe that Multer throws `MulterError: File too large` with error code `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`, even though the file size matches the configured limit.

**Expected behavior:** Multer should accept a file whose size exactly matches the configured `fileSize` limit.

**Actual behavior:** Multer rejects the file with `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`.
